sweeps.rationale: SD1.5 and SDXL settle at different step counts, so both baselines are shown; the anime model behaves like SDXL here and would only repeat it.
sweeps.caption: How many denoising steps the sampler takes. More steps cost more time, and stop helping well before they stop costing. With an ancestral sampler like this one, changing the count also reshuffles the scene a little.

stops.caption: Two steps is barely a start: coloured mush with a hint of where things will go.
Too few steps to resolve the scene: shapes are blocky and colour smears.
Shapes are arriving, but nothing has an edge yet.
The composition arrives, but edges and faces are still soft.
Most of the scene is legible. Fine detail is not.
Detail starts to settle and small features become readable.
Nearly settled, with the sampler still moving things about between counts.
Close to this model's best for the scene; most of what you will get is here.
Little is being added now beyond what this sampler reshuffles.
The common default. Quality has levelled off even as the scene shifts.
No better than 30, and the scene has drifted again on the way.
Different, not better, for well over twice the time and kudos.

sweeps.rationale: The same step counts held on a converging sampler, so the ancestral strip's drift can be seen against a scene that settles and stays put. It matches the ancestral strip's coverage model for model and scene for scene, because the step lesson should never be one a reader can only see through a sampler that re-rolls the image underneath it.
sweeps.caption: The same step counts on a converging sampler. Once the scene settles, extra steps stop moving it.

stops.caption: Two steps: the scene has not begun to form.
Too few steps for any sampler: the scene has not resolved at all.
A shape is emerging, still without detail.
A usable image appears, though the layout is still finding itself.
The composition is nearly decided, and from here it stays put.
The final composition is in place.
Detail firms up where it already is, without the scene moving.
Locked in. From here the scene stops moving.
Indistinguishable from 20 at a glance.
Compare with the ancestral strip at 30: nothing has reshuffled since 20.
No visible change, for a third more time and kudos.
All but identical to 30, for well over twice the time and kudos.

sweeps.rationale: SDXL burns out at a lower guidance than SD1.5, so the two baselines diverge; the anime model tracks SDXL closely enough that a third strip teaches nothing new.
sweeps.caption: How hard the model is pushed to follow your prompt. Too low and it ignores you; too high and it overcooks the image.

stops.caption: Guidance as good as off, and the lowest the horde accepts. The model paints what it likes and your prompt barely reaches it.
Barely steered. The prompt is a suggestion the model may take.
Loose adherence and soft colour, with room for the model's own ideas.
Gentle steering, and the subject you asked for is reliably there.
A gentle balance, good when your prompt is already detailed.
Comfortable adherence with colour still behaving.
The usual home base for most models.
Firmer adherence, with contrast beginning to climb.
Firmer still, and saturation is now visibly rising.
Hardening: edges crisp up past the point of looking natural.
Overcooked: harsh contrast, burnt colour and crunchy edges.
Far past useful. The image is being forced, and no part of that is better prompt-following.

sweeps.rationale: Ancestral and converging samplers separate differently on each baseline, so one photoreal SD1.5 model and one SDXL model cover the contrast at fixed steps.
sweeps.caption: Which algorithm walks the image out of noise. At the same steps and seed, each one lands somewhere slightly different.

stops.caption: Fast and predictable, and a good baseline to compare the others against.
Ancestral: it adds fresh noise each step, so the image keeps changing as you add steps.
Converges quickly and is often the cleanest result at 20 to 30 steps.
Stochastic, so it lands somewhere of its own, often with richer texture.

sweeps.rationale: Two mainstream models, where 2 and 3 visibly loosen the prompt. The anime model renders this scene as a photograph and taught nothing here, so it has its own strip on the anime scene instead.
sweeps.caption: How many layers to cut from the end of the text encoder. Anime-lineage models were trained expecting one to be cut.

stops.caption: The full text encoder. What most non-anime models expect.
Skips the last layer. On an anime-lineage model this is the intended setting; elsewhere it just loosens the prompt.
Skipping further loses prompt detail, and your wording starts to be ignored.

sweeps.rationale: The failure hires-fix repairs only appears above a model's native size, so the strip must render above it; at native size the flag does nothing at all. It runs on a figure rather than on the compact object it used to, because what goes wrong at oversize is that the model repeats what it knows, and on a person that reads as a second head or a third arm rather than as a general softness a reader has to be told to see. The frame is tall for the same reason: an SD1.5 model stacks a subject up a long frame rather than enlarging it. It runs on the default SD1.5 model rather than the photoreal one, which holds together at oversize well enough to hide the lesson.
sweeps.caption: Above a model's native size, one pass repeats what it knows. Hires-fix generates small first, then enlarges and refines.

stops.caption: One pass at the full size. Above what the model knows you get duplicated details and stretched shapes.
Generated small, then enlarged and re-diffused, so the composition stays coherent.

sweeps.rationale: The same reading on a model trained at 1024, and it breaks on a different shape of ask. SD1.5 stacks a subject up a long frame, so its pair renders tall; SDXL does not. At 1152x2048 and again at 1536x3072, three times its training height, one pass still composed a single clean figure and the pair had nothing to teach. What breaks SDXL is square area: at 2048x2048 it puts two heads on one body, and the pair runs at 2304x2304 so it is clearly past that edge rather than sitting on it. That the two baselines fail on different shapes is why both carry a pair.
sweeps.caption: Above a model's native size, one pass repeats what it knows. Hires-fix generates small first, then enlarges and refines.

stops.caption: One pass at the full size. Above what the model knows you get duplicated details and stretched shapes.
Generated small, then enlarged and re-diffused, so the composition stays coherent.

sweeps.rationale: The texture strip is the one that teaches: seams are invisible on a single object and unmistakable on a repeating surface, which is what anyone actually tiles. Seam behaviour is a sampler-level effect that reads the same on every baseline, so one model is enough.
sweeps.caption: Whether the edges are made to wrap. Shown as a three-by-three plate beside the single tile, because a seam only exists where one copy meets the next.

stops.caption: The edges end wherever the image happened to stop, so every join is a hard line.
The edges are made to wrap, so the grain and the gaps run on across each join.

sweeps.rationale: The counter-example, kept deliberately: tiling is a property of the edges, not a way to make a picture repeatable. A centred object tiles into a grid of that object however the flag is set, which is the mistake the texture strip is there to correct.
sweeps.caption: The same flag on a scene with a subject in the middle. The edges do wrap, but a picture of one thing repeats as a grid of that thing either way: tiling makes edges meet, it does not make an image into a texture.

stops.caption: Repeated as-is: hard seams, and a robot in every square.
The seams are gone and the robot is still in every square. This is not what tiling is for.

sweeps.rationale: SDXL only, because the degradation being taught is SDXL-specific: it is what happens when you ask an SDXL model for the sizes an SD1.5 model was built for.
sweeps.caption: Every model has a size it was trained at. Ask an SDXL model for much less and it does not simply get smaller, it gets worse.

stops.caption: Far below anything SDXL saw in training: the image collapses into mush.
The scene survives but the subject does not: the courier is gone.
Anatomy holds, but the framing collapses to a cramped close-up of whatever fits.
Most of the scene is back. The last of the crowding clears in the next stop.
SDXL's native size. This is what the model was trained to make.

sweeps.rationale: One grid per baseline, because steps and guidance interact differently for SD1.5 and for SDXL.
sweeps.caption: Steps and guidance are not independent. Read across for guidance and down for steps: both have to be in range before an image looks right. The scene also drifts down each column: this sampler re-rolls details as steps change.

sweeps.rationale: The third baseline of the same grid, on the anime model and therefore on the anime scene: the tag idiom that lineage was trained on is part of what its guidance range means, so reading it against a photoreal prompt would measure the prompt rather than the model.
sweeps.caption: Steps and guidance are not independent. Read across for guidance and down for steps: both have to be in range before an image looks right. The scene also drifts down each column: this sampler re-rolls details as steps change.

sweeps.rationale: Which sampler to choose is really a question about how it behaves as the step count changes, and no single strip can show that. Both baselines run it because SDXL settles at different step counts than SD1.5.
sweeps.caption: Read across a row to see what more steps buy that sampler. The ancestral and SDE rows never settle: they re-roll the detail at every step count, so the image keeps changing rather than improving. The other two rows stop moving once the scene has converged. That contrast is the whole point.

sweeps.rationale: The failure this repairs is a property of the size you ask for, so it has to be read down a column of sizes rather than from a single pair. The off column doubles as the oversize anti-example: it is what asking an SD1.5 model for a large image actually looks like, duplicated subjects and all. The bottom row is four times the model's training size, past where the repair rescues anything, so the grid answers how far this carries as well as what it does. It runs on the default SD1.5 model, which breaks at oversize where the photoreal one holds together and hides the lesson.
sweeps.caption: Read down the off column to see what asking for more pixels than the model was trained on does: the scene stops being one scene and starts repeating, which on a person means a second head or a third arm. The on column generates small first, then enlarges and re-diffuses, so the composition survives the size. Read to the bottom row to see the repair run out.

rows.caption: Requested size, top to bottom. This model was trained at 512.

sweeps.rationale: The same grid an octave up. SDXL degrades more gently and later, so the sizes that show it are its own, and the bottom row is well past what any of these models were trained for.
sweeps.caption: The same lesson on a model trained at 1024. It takes a larger ask to break it, and it breaks the same way: repeated features rather than a bigger picture. The bottom row is where the second pass stops being able to compose what the first one asked for.

rows.caption: Requested size, top to bottom. This model was trained at 1024.

sweeps.rationale: The pair strip shows that the schedule matters at 10 steps; only a grid shows the part that matters more, which is that the advantage shrinks as the step count rises. Held on a converging sampler for the same reason the pair is.
sweeps.caption: Read down the rows: the gap between the two columns is wide where steps are scarce and closes as they are not. Karras is a way of spending few steps well, not a setting that is better in general.

columns.caption: The plain schedule, then the Karras one.

sweeps.rationale: Denoising strength only means anything when there is a source image, so this is the one sweep that renders image-to-image. The source is the signed-off render of this world's deck scene, and the prompt is the same scene in different weather, so a reader is watching one picture they have already met being restyled rather than meeting two strangers at once.

sweeps.rationale: Rendered on the close portrait because hands and anatomy are where a negative prompt does visible work, and the scene asks for bare fingers on purpose: gloves hide the very thing the strip is about. SDXL only, having tried the SD1.5 model: at 512 the hands are too small in frame for the repair to read, and a strip whose lesson needs pointing at is not worth the render.
sweeps.caption: A second prompt naming what to steer away from. It is not a quality switch: it conditions the other half of the guidance the model is already doing, and what it changes first is usually anatomy, hands most of all.
sweeps.negative_prompt: extra fingers, fused fingers, missing fingers, deformed hands, mutated hands, extra limbs, bad anatomy

stops.caption: No negative prompt: whatever the model does with the hands is what you get.

sweeps.rationale: The other thing a negative prompt does, and the one that is easiest to check: naming a thing that is in the picture and having it leave. The scene names its removable parts on purpose, so a reader can count them in the first stop and count them again in the second.
sweeps.caption: The same control used to take something out rather than to fix something. What you name is steered away from, which is why a negative prompt is worth reading as a list of things you do not want in frame rather than as a quality setting.

sweeps.rationale: Attention weights are the one piece of prompt syntax worth teaching early, and a style token is the clearest place to see one: the whole image changes together, so there is nothing else to mistake the effect for. Rendered on the SD1.5 model, which responds to style tokens strongly enough for the low end of the range to still read.
sweeps.caption: Putting (a phrase:weight) in a prompt changes how hard that phrase pulls. Below 1 it is a hint, above 1 it starts to dominate, and past about 1.5 it stops adding style and starts taking the picture apart.

stops.caption: Half weight: a hint of the style over an otherwise ordinary render.
Present but restrained, which is where you want a style you are blending.
Just under plain weight, and already clearly the style you asked for.
Weight 1 is what the phrase would do with no parentheses at all.
A nudge up, which is usually all a style token needs.
The style now leads and the scene follows it.
The top of the usable range: washes are winning and structure is starting to go.
The anti-example. At double weight the phrase overwhelms everything else you asked for.

sweeps.rationale: The half of weighting that a single rising token cannot teach: two phrases pulling against each other, where what matters is the ratio and not either number. Written so the two weights always sum to 2, which makes the strip a crossfade rather than a volume knob.
sweeps.caption: Weights are a balance between the things you asked for, not a volume control on each. Here two seasons are held in one prompt and traded off across the strip: neither is ever removed, and the picture lands wherever the ratio puts it.

sweeps.rationale: eta is the first solver knob the horde exposes and the only one with a code-level claim attached: at zero an SDE sampler has no noise left to inject, so it should land where its deterministic twin does. The ladder exists so that can be seen rather than asserted.

sweeps.rationale: s_noise scales the fresh noise an ancestral or SDE sampler adds back on each step; eta decides whether noise is added, s_noise how loud it is. The ladder is on the ancestral Euler so the effect is not confounded with a solver correction.

sweeps.rationale: Denoising strength inside a mask, which is the control the masked mode adds and the one inpainting does not really have. The backend encodes the whole picture and then restricts where noise is applied, so what was under the mask is still there to be redrawn by this much; inpainting erases the masked pixels before encoding and has nothing left to vary. It runs on the deck render a reader has already met on the image-to-image page, with the coat masked and the scene's own prompt, so the only question on screen is how much of that coat survives.
sweeps.caption: The same strength control as image-to-image, acting only where the mask is. Low, and the masked part is the one that was already there; high, and it is redrawn from nothing. Everything outside the mask stays exactly as it came in at every stop.

stops.caption: Barely touched. The coat under the mask is the one that was already there.

sweeps.rationale: The horde has two ways to redraw part of a picture and they are different pipelines, not two names for one. Masked image-to-image encodes the whole source and restricts where noise lands, so the masked pixels are still the starting point; inpainting erases them first and grows the mask before encoding. Everything here is held apart from those two facts: one model, one source, one mask, one prompt, and one ordinary checkpoint rather than an inpainting one, because the horde runs whichever model was asked for and only requires the worker to keep an inpainting model on hand. Read across for the difference and down for where it stops mattering.
sweeps.caption: The same mask over the same picture, put through both of the horde's masked modes. The left column keeps what was under the mask and redraws it by the strength on that row, so the strength is a real dial. The right column throws it away before it starts, which is why the top right cell is a flat patch: at that strength there is not enough of the pass left to put anything back. Below the row where it can finish, inpainting does not give you a gentler edit; it gives you an unfinished one.

rows.caption: The strength asked for, top to bottom. Only the left column can act on it.

sweeps.rationale: Outpainting is the one mode with nothing of its own in the payload. The backends select the same pipeline for it as for inpainting, byte for byte, and nothing anywhere pads a canvas: the caller pads the picture and masks what it added. So these stops vary the input rather than a parameter, each one a canvas padded beforehand and checked in beside its mask, and each stating the size of its own canvas because the backend resizes a source to the requested dimensions and would otherwise squeeze the padding straight back out. What a reader is choosing is how much they are asking the model to invent, which is the only real dial here.
sweeps.caption: Pushing the edges of a picture outwards. The middle is the render the strip starts from and every stop keeps it untouched; what changes is how much new canvas the model is asked to fill on either side.

stops.caption: A narrow border each side. There is enough of the deck in view for the model to carry the railing, the canopy and the sky straight out.
Half the picture again. The scene still holds together, and the new edges are inventing rather than repeating what is beside them.

The canvas is twice what it was and half of what you are looking at was never in the original. It still reads as one place, and you can find the joins: a faint vertical seam where the picture that was sent meets the canvas around it.

sweeps.rationale: One example per ControlNet guidance mode, on the world the ControlNet tutorial itself uses: a photographed person with a face, hands, a horizon and a lot of straight ironwork, which is the scene most of the detectors have something to find in. The source, the map the detector drew and the render it guided are published together because the map is the thing a reader is choosing between and the render alone cannot show it. Everything but the mode is held: one model, one seed, one prompt, one strength, the same source at 512. Deliberate and 512 because the horde serves ControlNet on SD1.5 alone. The maps are drawn on horde-image-utilities, the same detector code an alchemist worker runs, rather than approximated by anything else.

stops.caption: Canny drew a single clean outline for everything it could find: the wires of the railing, the fittings on the mast, the folds of the coat and the line of the hills. The render keeps all of it in place and changes only what an outline cannot say, so the coat comes back brown instead of teal and the goggles become spectacles.

hed draws softer, thicker strokes and lets the small detail go, so the railing survives as a few bars and the face is barely described. The render holds the pose and the horizon and takes the rest for itself: a warmer sky, a tan coat, teal in the hair.

pidinet keeps the heavy boundaries and empties out the interior, leaving the head, the coat and the railing as flat shapes. The render fills those shapes with its own picture, and the airship envelope comes back as a pale sail.

teed finds fine line everywhere, including the edges of the clouds and the panels of the envelope. The render follows it closely and reads as a pen drawing with colour washed over it, with the envelope drawn as a ribbed gold balloon.

pyracanny gives the same complete outline as canny with a softer edge to it. The render keeps the whole scene, down to the wires of the railing and the curve of the deck, and spends its freedom on colour.

binary reduces the photograph to black and white with no grey between, so the coat becomes one mass and the face is lost. The render invents a face to fill the gap and reads the speckle under the railing as boats on water.
scribble reduces the picture to a few coarse strokes. The render keeps the standing figure and the railing, closes the eyes it had to invent, and turns the envelope into a plain white shape.

fakescribbles traces the main shapes in thick rounded strokes and puts nothing inside them. The pose and the deck hold, the railing comes back as wire mesh, and the goggles become an earpiece against the hair.

scribble_xdog keeps more than the other scribble modes: an inked, grainy line that still carries the folds of the coat and the rails. The render stays close to the source and reads as a drawing made with a dry pen.

scribble_pidinet is the loosest map here, a few beaded strokes with the interior gone. The render invents most of what it shows: rigging ropes where the mast was, birds in the sky, fur on the collar and the cuffs.

standard_lineart carries tone as well as line, so the clouds, the hills and the folds of the coat all arrive as shading. The render stays closer to the source than any other line mode here and adds only small things of its own, such as the pines below the railing.

lineart draws a thin, even outline and leaves the shading out. The render keeps the composition and softens everything else, so the envelope becomes a pale balloon and a second airship appears in the distance.
lineart_anime draws a clean line and hatches the large flat areas. The render keeps the scene and answers the hatching with a ribbed envelope and a dark sea.

lineart_anime_denoise clears the faint lines away and keeps the confident ones, so the face is barely in the map at all. The render holds the pose and the horizon and puts its own face, its own coat and a fan-shaped envelope over them.

mlsd finds straight lines and nothing else: the mast, the rails and the edges of the deck. The woman is missing from the map entirely, so the ironwork arrives exactly and she is redrawn from the prompt.
depth reports how far away things are and says nothing about what they are. The figure and the railing keep their distances, and the sea of clouds is rebuilt as water with a pale hull lying in it.
midas_depth reads the sky as empty and cuts the figure sharply out of it. The standing shape and the railing hold, and the view is invented: headlands, houses and a small boat.

zoe_depth gives a flatter reading, with less distance between the figure and everything behind her. The silhouette still holds, and the softer background fills with hills, floating ice and a ribbed envelope.
depth_anything cuts the figure out crisply and leaves the background dark. The silhouette comes through exactly, and everything behind it is the prompt's invention.

depth_anything_v2 models the folds of the coat and the curve of the envelope rather than a flat cut-out. The render follows that modelling and stays closest to the source of the depth modes, with the envelope drawn as a ribbed hull.

normal reports which way each surface faces, and on this photograph it comes back noisy, with the sky flattened to a single colour. The render holds the figure and the railing and rebuilds the view behind them.

normal_bae reads the same surfaces cleanly: the shoulders, the sleeves and the folds face the way they do in the source. The render keeps that modelling and invents the sea, the rocks and the small boat.

openpose keeps the body and throws the world away, leaving shoulders, arms, hips and a few points of the face on black. The stance survives and everything else changes, so the open deck becomes the inside of a cabin.

seg paints the picture into labelled regions, with the figure as one block and the sky, the water and the deck as others. The render respects the blocks and fills them freely, turning the envelope into a balloon and a drum.

oneformer_ade20k gives cleaner regions than seg and separates the sky, the land, the water and the deck. The render keeps that layout band for band and invents the contents, including a village under the railing.
oneformer_coco works from coarser labels and merges what ade20k separates. The layout still arrives, and with less to go on the render makes the deck a hull and the land a bank of scrub.

color reduces the photograph to a grid of its colours and keeps none of its shapes: cream sky at the top, the teal of the coat, a band of dark below. The render builds a fresh picture out of that palette, and the courier comes back seated beside a cabin window with a box of flowers next to her.

shuffle stirs the picture into loops of itself, with her head, the railing and the ring of the airship smeared around the turns. The render keeps the colours and the round shapes and puts them somewhere new, with goggles, banks of cloud and a sea with one small boat on it.

recolor_luminance is the source in grey with every tone kept, which leaves almost nothing to invent. The render is the photograph again with new colour in it, and the ink and watercolour the prompt asked for barely shows.
recolor_intensity measures brightness differently and holds the picture just as tightly. The render is the source recoloured once more, with the coat split between tan and teal.
tile hands the render a blurred copy of the picture itself. Every shape is held and the work left is to sharpen it, which the render does in the prompt's own brush and wash.
tile_ttplanet_guided passes the picture through almost untouched. The render repaints it line for line, and the goggles, the belt and the wires of the railing all survive the change of medium.
tile_ttplanet_simple hands over the picture with no blur at all. The hold is the tightest in this gallery: the same scene, the same pose and the same light, painted rather than photographed.

sweeps.rationale: The same walk through every guidance mode on an illustrated source, which several of the detectors were trained for and several others were not. The anime line detectors have something to find here that world 1 never gave them, and the depth and surface detectors have much less. Anything Diffusion, at clip skip 2, because ControlNet is SD1.5 only and the booru dialect needs the anime checkpoint.

pidinet keeps only the strong boundaries, and the face and the folds of the haori go with the rest. The render keeps the seated shape and the steps and paints its own face and its own gold sash.
teed finds fine line everywhere, including each maple leaf on the stone. The render follows it closely and gives the most detailed reading of the source in this group, down to the wet steps.
pyracanny outlines as completely as canny with a softer edge to it. The render keeps the whole scene and spends its freedom on colour, which drains to grey with the red of the hakama kept.

binary reduces the drawing to black and white, and the face, the hair and the fox tail fall into one mass. The render keeps the seated figure and the pillars and rebuilds the trees as a shrine in mist.
scribble leaves a coarse black and white reduction of the picture. The pose and the steps survive, and the maples behind are replaced with a corridor of torii gates.
fakescribbles traces the main shapes in thick rounded strokes. The seated figure holds, and the trees become a wall of gates in fog.
scribble_xdog leaves a fine grainy line that still carries the folds of the cloth and the edges of the steps. The render stays close to the source and sets props of its own on the stone.
scribble_pidinet gives the loosest strokes here and loses the boundary between the figure and the ground. The render keeps the pose and dresses it differently, in black over white.
standard_lineart carries shading as well as line, so the trees, the steps and the cloth all arrive with weight. The render stays close to the source and warms the maples to pink.
lineart draws a thin even line and leaves the shading out. The render keeps the pose, the steps and the dark hair the source has, and lets the season drift towards pink.

lineart_anime draws the clean line this kind of drawing was made for, and it catches the ears, the tail and the fall of the hair. The render keeps all of it and changes little more than the colour of the maples.
lineart_anime_denoise clears the faint lines away first, so the map is sparser. The render keeps the pose and the steps and adds furniture of its own, including a pair of standing lanterns.

mlsd finds the pillars, the crossbeam and the edges of the steps, and finds nothing of the girl or the fox. The render keeps that architecture and builds a different picture inside it, with the figure seen from behind on a long stair.
depth reports distance alone, and here it does keep the ears and the tail as part of the near shape. The render holds that silhouette and rebuilds the gates, the trees and the leaves around it.
midas_depth separates the figure from a flat dark background. The seated shape holds and the setting is invented, with red cloth laid across the steps.
zoe_depth reads the scene more softly, with the tail barely separated from the stone. The render keeps the shape and gives the background less structure than the other depth modes do.
depth_anything cuts the figure, the ears and the tail out cleanly. The silhouette arrives exactly, and the railing, the trees and the mist behind it are the render's own.
depth_anything_v2 models the hair and the folds rather than a flat cut-out, and the render follows it closely. It gives the truest seat and posture of the depth modes on this drawing.
normal comes back noisy on a drawing that has no real lighting in it, with flat patches where it could not decide. The render still holds the figure and invents a shrine roof and a hanging lantern.

normal_bae is soft and almost featureless here, because a flat illustration gives a surface detector very little to read. The render keeps the pose loosely, adds a large bow, and moves the scene indoors.
openpose finds the body and nothing else: no ears, no tail, no shrine. The seat and the reach of the arm hold, and everything that makes her a fox keeper comes from the prompt.
seg labels the picture into regions and mislabels several of them on a drawing. The render keeps the block layout and reads the steps as the floor of a wooden hall.
oneformer_ade20k gives clean regions: the figure, the two pillars, the ground and the trees. The render keeps that arrangement and fills the trees with a corridor of gates.
oneformer_coco labels the same scene more coarsely and loses the figure into one flat shape. The layout still holds, and the render puts its own keeper and its own maples inside it.

color keeps a grid of the drawing's colours and none of its shapes: white, vermilion, cream and a little navy. The render spends that palette on an arrangement of its own, a row of torii running back into the trees, and hands the keeper white hair along with everything else.

shuffle stirs the drawing into loops of itself, the maples and the black hair wound around white spirals. The render takes the same colours into a colder scene, with pale trees behind the gate and the keeper sitting silver-haired on the steps.
recolor_luminance is the drawing in grey with every tone intact, so the render has only the colour left to decide. It returns the scene exactly, with the black hair and the red hakama the source has.
recolor_intensity measures brightness differently and holds the picture just as tightly. The colour comes back thinner here, with a gold sash and pale leaves.
tile hands over a blurred copy of the drawing itself. The render sharpens it back and paints in the detail the blur had lost, including the grain of the steps and the leaves on them.
tile_ttplanet_guided passes the drawing through almost unchanged. The render repaints it faithfully and sets shrine buildings behind the trees.
tile_ttplanet_simple hands over the picture untouched, and the render is the source again in ink and wash, with the same pose, the same tail and the same fallen leaves.

sweeps.rationale: The third world is here to show the detectors failing honestly. Nothing in it has a human skeleton, so the pose detector has nothing to return, and the scene is close, soft and shallow, so the long-range depth detectors have much less to separate than the deck did. A reader deciding whether a mode suits their picture is better served by seeing what an empty map looks like than by reading that one is possible.

pidinet keeps the boundaries and empties the interior. The render answers with a cartoon, putting two eyes, a nose and a mouth where the ports and the seams were.
teed finds fine line across the whole picture, including the foliage and the water at the tap. The render follows it closely and keeps the machine looking like a machine.
pyracanny outlines as completely as canny with a softer edge to it. The render holds the pots, the planters and the skyline exactly while painting them freely.

scribble leaves a few coarse strokes and no surface at all. The render turns the machine into a character with a face and wheels and keeps only the pots and the skyline from the source.
fakescribbles traces the main shapes in thick rounded strokes. The stance and the pots hold, the shell comes back green, and the lens ports become eyes again.
scribble_xdog keeps a finer, grainier line and more of the surface with it. The render stays closer to the machine and sets sunflowers over its head.

lineart_anime keeps a clean line over the whole picture. The render holds the machine and the rooftop and reads them as a drawing rather than a photograph.
lineart_anime_denoise drops the faint lines and keeps the strong ones. The render holds the shape and the pots and puts sunflowers where the source has leaves.

mlsd finds the roof edges, the planters and the buildings, and finds nothing of the robot at all. The rooftop arrives exactly and the machine is rebuilt from the prompt as something else, with a helmet for a head and an apron over its body.
depth gives the rounded mass of the robot and the lumps of the plants without a single marking. The render keeps the volumes and paints a smiling face onto them.
midas_depth reads the same volumes more coarsely. The render keeps the round body and puts one large eye where the map left a shadow.
zoe_depth flattens the scene, with the robot barely separated from the pots. The render keeps the mass and gives it a single green eye, because the map never said there were three ports.
depth_anything separates the robot and the plants crisply. The three ports come back and the shell keeps the source's shape, with the colour left to the prompt.
depth_anything_v2 models the dome and the leaves rather than a flat cut-out. It gives the most faithful robot of the depth modes, orange again and with all three lenses.
normal comes back noisy on this photograph, with the sky flattened to a single colour. The render still keeps the shell, the arms and the pots and repaints the rooftop behind them.

normal_bae reads the dome, the arms and the pots as surfaces facing where they face in the source. The render keeps that modelling and changes little more than the colour of the lenses and the plants.
openpose found no person here, so the map it drew is empty black. With nothing to hold, the render keeps only what the prompt asked for and builds a different machine on a different rooftop.
seg labels the picture and splits the robot across several regions, so the shell arrives in pieces. The render keeps the pots and the greenery in place and reassembles the machine its own way.
oneformer_ade20k reads the robot as one region, with the sky, the hedges and the floor around it. The render keeps that arrangement and paints a wide-eyed machine into the shape.
oneformer_coco has no label that fits a gardening robot, so it hands over a shape among the foliage. The layout holds, and the render fills the shape with a crowned machine and hoses for arms.

color holds a grid of the picture's colours and none of its shapes: cream across the top, orange and brown through the middle, one square of bright blue. The render gives that palette to a different machine, orange shelled with a blue arm and a blue wheel, clipping a bed of plants.

shuffle stirs the photograph into loops of itself, shell, lenses and leaves wound round the sunset. The render keeps every colour and spends it on another robot, pale green in the body with orange rings painted across it and the city behind gone hazy.

recolor_luminance is the photograph in grey with every tone kept, which leaves the render only the colour to choose. It comes back as the photograph again, orange shell and blue lenses, with none of the ink and wash the prompt asked for.
recolor_intensity measures brightness differently and holds the picture just as tightly. The result is the same photograph once more, with cooler colour in it.

tile hands over a heavily blurred copy of the picture. Every shape is held and the work left is to put the detail back, which the render does in ink and wash, with flowers and grass where the blur said nothing.
tile_ttplanet_guided passes the picture through almost untouched, and the render repaints it faithfully: the same shell, the same three lenses and the same pots, in the medium the prompt asked for.
tile_ttplanet_simple hands over the picture with no blur at all, and the hold is the tightest in this gallery. The render is the rooftop again, painted instead of photographed.

sweeps.rationale: The strength dial read against a map of hard edges, which is the mode most readers meet first and the one whose grip is easiest to see: an edge either survives into the render or it does not. The stops are the ones the QR strength strip already walks, so the two can be read against each other. The horde takes control_strength alongside a control type or the QR code workflow and refuses a request that sets it with neither, and only a recently updated worker is handed a job that carries it.
sweeps.caption: Canny's outline is already in charge at the lowest strength here, so all eight stops keep the same railing, the same coat and the same face. What rises with the number is how literally the render follows the line: the sky flattens into bands, the fittings on the mast are sanded away and the brushwork tightens onto the edges. Nothing in this range breaks, so the lower stops are the useful ones and the higher stops only cost the render its own ideas.

stops.caption: The loosest of the eight. There is real weather in the sky, a white cloud out over the water, and the coat is painted with visible brush rather than filled in.
Almost the same picture with the cloud thinned. The sky is starting to settle into flat bands of peach and grey.
The wash tightens onto the outline. The hills behind the railing lose their mottling and the hair picks up the teal the earpiece had.
The middle of the strip and a fair place to work: the rails and the deck edge are where the map put them, and the picture still looks painted.
The fittings begin to go. There are fewer buttons down the coat than there were and the horizon is one clean edge.
The brushwork has pulled in to the lines. The sleeve is flat brown with a single gold stroke on it, and there is no cloud left in the sky.
Little is left to give up. The hills are flat colour between drawn edges and the collar has lost its shading.
The strictest reading of the outline: every edge is honoured and the areas between them are filled rather than painted. Nothing has broken, and nothing has been gained since 1.4.

sweeps.rationale: The strength dial read against a map that holds only long straight lines. The deck's railing and rigging are the whole of what this detector kept, so the strip is a reading of how hard a sparse map can pull. The stops are the ones the QR strength strip already walks, so the two can be read against each other. The horde takes control_strength alongside a control type or the QR code workflow and refuses a request that sets it with neither, and only a recently updated worker is handed a job that carries it.
sweeps.caption: Straight lines are all this map holds, so the woman is redrawn at every stop and only the ironwork answers to the number. At 1.25 the railing is loosely painted and the deck curves where the render wants it to; by 1.4 the rails are ruled and the deck edge is straight; at the top the frame of the envelope looks drafted rather than drawn. Around 1.4 keeps the architecture true while the rest of the picture still looks painted.

stops.caption: Loose ironwork. The rail bars wander, the deck boards curve away, and the vessel out over the water is a woven basket the render invented.
The rails begin to line up and a white hull replaces the basket. The deck edge still bends where the render wanted it to.
The railing is drawn bar by bar now and the deck edge has straightened out. The clouds are still doing as they please.
The architecture is true: rails ruled, deck edge straight, mast upright. Everything else is still painted loosely, which is what makes this a fair place to work.
Little changes in the ironwork, so the render spends the stop above it, running a cable out of the frame and flattening the vessel into a deck with windows.
The straight lines are now hard enough to pull the airship into being: a ribbed envelope over the rail, drawn with the same ruled edges.
The envelope is drafted rather than drawn, and an orange seat has grown in the near corner where the map had a straight edge and nothing else.
The strictest stop. Every long edge in the picture is a ruled line, including the seams of the envelope, and the woman is the only thing left that looks hand-drawn.

sweeps.rationale: The strength dial read against distance rather than line. A depth map states where things sit rather than where their edges are, so what tightens as the dial climbs is the arrangement of the scene rather than its drawing. The stops are the ones the QR strength strip already walks, so the two can be read against each other. The horde takes control_strength alongside a control type or the QR code workflow and refuses a request that sets it with neither, and only a recently updated worker is handed a job that carries it.
sweeps.caption: The depth map holds the figure at every stop, so what the number changes is everything behind her. Low, the view is invented freely, with an island and a boat out in the water; high, the background settles into the flat layers the map describes and the envelope becomes a plain pale shape. The picture never stops looking painted, and 1.35 to 1.45 keeps the invention without letting the layers go slack.

stops.caption: The loosest of the eight. The map asked for a near figure and a far view, and the render answers with a headland, a small boat and a bank of drawn cloud.
The same freedom with a little more order. The boats are still out there and the envelope is still woven basketwork.
The headland goes. The water resolves into the broad layers of distance the map describes, and the envelope loses its weave.
The view behind her is layered rather than invented, and the cloud bank is the last piece of the render's own drawing left in it.
A small town reappears on the far shore. The layers around it are flatter than at 1.35, so what survives here is a detail rather than a place.
The water is a set of flat steps going back, with a low island sitting on one of them. Nothing has broken; the picture has simply stopped adding.
The layers go slack. What was a sea is bands of grey and blue with a few rocks on them.
The strictest reading of distance: pale flat planes stacked to the horizon and an envelope with no surface at all. The woman is unchanged, which is the whole point of this strip.

sweeps.rationale: The strength dial read against which way each surface faces. Almost the same picture, warmer in the sky. The rocks under the railing keep the pink the render put there.
A fur collar grows where the map had a raised surface. The clouds are still drawn rather than washed.
The drawn clouds go. The sky is a set of pale streaks and the ornament on the chain is thinning out.
One medallion left. The shape out on the water has settled into a plain white hull with nothing on it.

What the number buys is the stance: at 1.25 the arm reaches oddly and the shoulders drift, and from 1.4 up the pose settles into the one the map describes and stays there. Use the top of the range when the pose is what matters, and expect the setting to come from the prompt at any strength.

The shoulders square up and the arm shortens to something a body could do. The cabin has been rebuilt again, with a wooden bench where the print was.
The hand finds the window frame and holds it. The pose is close to the map now, and everything around it has changed once more.
The stance settles: shoulders level, head upright, one hand at the frame. This is the first stop that returns the pose the map describes.
The same stance again, so the difference is all in the room. A bird crosses the water outside and the wall behind her has gone orange.

stops.caption: The regions are already in charge: sky, water, deck and figure sit where the map puts them. Inside them the render is free, so the water is scattered ice and a roof leans in at the edge.
A row of houses grows in the block the map marked as building. The ice on the water is still loosely painted.
The far shore gains a town and a stack of crates appears under the railing. The boundary between water and land is sharper than it was.
The edges harden. The floes flatten into shapes with outlines and the buildings line up along the far side of the water.
Panels with writing on them fill the block by the railing. Anything the map called one region is now one flat colour.
The water is flat plates on flat blue and the town is a strip. The picture has begun to read as a plan of a place rather than a view of one.
The panels are framed in arches and the sky is banded. Little is left inside each region for the brush to do.
The strictest stop, and the flattest: the sea is brown shapes on blue, the shore is a band, and the boundaries the map drew are the strongest lines in the picture.

sweeps.rationale: The strength dial read against a map that is the picture itself. This is the mode with the least room between guidance and copying, which is what the top of the range is here to show. The stops are the ones the QR strength strip already walks, so the two can be read against each other. The horde takes control_strength alongside a control type or the QR code workflow and refuses a request that sets it with neither, and only a recently updated worker is handed a job that carries it.
sweeps.caption: The map is the picture itself, so the hold is total at every stop and the difference between them is small. Low, the render still paints: the coat is recoloured, the sky is redrawn and the brush is visible. High, it narrows onto the source's own colours and edges until the ink and watercolour of the prompt is a thin layer over a copy. For repainting something in a new style, stay at the bottom of this range.

stops.caption: The most painted of the eight. The wash runs loose over the coat, the wrist is a dark cuff rather than a glove, and the hills beyond the railing are soft.
Nearly the same picture, with the hand read as a mitten and the edge of the collar drawn a little firmer.
The belt and its buckle come back the way the source has them. The brushwork is still visible across the coat.
A brooch appears at the throat and the buttons down the front line up. The picture is tightening onto the source rather than changing.
The distant hull on the water sharpens into a shape with a wake behind it, and the coat keeps its white patches of light.
The envelope over the deck darkens and its ribs show. Small marks are turning into drawn detail.
The paint thins. Edges that were two washes meeting at 1.25 are lines here, and the hair has lost its softest strokes.
The strictest stop, and the closest to a copy: brass rims on the goggles, hard edges on the coat, and a wash thin enough to read the photograph through.
